danish.title: Trettende bog (1812) — Kapitel 13
paragraphs: Den franske evakuering begyndte natten mellem den sjette og syvende oktober: køkkener og skure blev revet ned, vogne lastet, og tropper og bagagetog satte sig i bevægelse.
Klokken syv om morgenen stod en fransk kolonne i marchuniform — med tschakkoer, geværer, rygsække og enorme sække — foran skurene, og livlig fransk tale blandet med eder lød langs hele rækken.

I skuret var alle klar, påklædt, opspændt og med sko på, og de ventede blot på ordren til at marchere. Den syge soldat, Sokolov, bleg og mager med mørke ringe under øjnene, sad alene på sin plads, barfodet og uklædt. Hans øjne, der stod frem i det afmagrede ansigt, stirrede spørgende på kammeraterne, som ikke bemærkede ham, og han stønnede jævnt og stille. Det var tydeligvis ikke så meget hans lidelser, der fik ham til at stønne — han havde dysenteri — som frygten for og sorgen over at blive efterladt alene.

Pierre, med et reb om livet og iført sko, som Karatajev (Platon Karatajev) havde lavet til ham af et stykke læder, en fransk soldat havde revet af en tekiste og bragt for at få sine støvler repareret, gik hen til den syge mand og satte sig på hug ved siden af ham.
»Ved du hvad, Sokolov, de tager ikke alle sammen af sted! De har et hospital her. Du har det måske bedre end os andre,« sagde Pierre.
»Åh Gud! Åh, det bliver min død! Åh Gud!« stønnede manden med højere stemme.
»Jeg går lige hen og spørger dem igen,« sagde Pierre, rejste sig og gik hen mod skurets dør.

Netop som Pierre nåede døren, kom korporalen, der dagen før havde tilbudt ham en pibe, hen til den med to soldater. Korporalen og soldaterne bar marchudstyr med rygsække og tschakkoer med metalremme, og det forandrede deres velkendte ansigter.
Korporalen kom efter ordre for at lukke døren. Fangerne skulle tælles, før de blev lukket ud.
»Korporal, hvad gør de med den syge mand?...« begyndte Pierre.

Men allerede mens han talte, begyndte han at tvivle på, om dette var den korporal, han kendte, eller en fremmed — så ulig sig selv virkede korporalen i det øjeblik. Desuden, netop som Pierre talte, lød der pludselig en skarp trommerullen fra begge sider. Korporalen rynkede brynene ad Pierres ord og smækkede døren i med nogle meningsløse eder. Skuret blev halvmørkt, og den skarpe trommerullen fra begge sider overdøvede den syge mands stønnen.

»Dér er den!... Der er den igen!...« sagde Pierre til sig selv, og et ufrivilligt gys løb ned ad hans ryg. I korporalens forandrede ansigt, i lyden af hans stemme, i trommernes oprørende og bedøvende larm genkendte han den mystiske, følelsesløse kraft, der tvang mennesker imod deres vilje til at dræbe deres medmennesker — den kraft, hvis virkning han havde været vidne til under henrettelserne. At frygte den eller forsøge at flygte fra den, at rette bønner eller formaninger til dem, der tjente som dens redskaber, var nyttesløst. Det vidste Pierre nu. Man måtte vente og holde ud. Han gik ikke hen til den syge igen, vendte sig ikke engang for at se på ham, men blev stående og stirrede mørkt ved skurets dør.

Da døren blev åbnet, og fangerne, trængende mod hinanden som en fåreflok, pressede sig ud, skubbede Pierre sig fremad og nærmede sig netop den kaptajn, som korporalen havde forsikret ham var villig til at gøre hvad som helst for ham. Kaptajnen var også i marchudstyr, og på hans kolde ansigt viste sig det samme det, som Pierre havde genkendt i korporalens ord og trommernes rullen.
»Videre, videre!« gentog kaptajnen barsk med rynkede bryn og betragtede de fanger, der trængte forbi ham.
Pierre gik hen til ham, selvom han vidste, at forsøget ville være forgæves.
»Hvad nu?« spurgte officeren med et koldt blik, som om han ikke genkendte Pierre.
Pierre fortalte ham om den syge mand.
»Han klarer nok at gå, for pokker!« sagde kaptajnen. »Videre, videre!« fortsatte han uden at se på Pierre.
»Men han er ved at dø,« begyndte Pierre igen.
»Vær nu så venlig...« råbte kaptajnen med et vredt blik.
»Dram-da-da-dam, dam-dam...« rullede trommerne, og Pierre forstod, at denne mystiske kraft fuldstændig beherskede disse mænd, og at det nu var nyttesløst at sige mere.
Officersfangerne blev adskilt fra soldaterne og beordret til at marchere forrest. Der var omkring tredive officerer, Pierre iblandt, og omkring tre hundrede menige.

Officererne, der var kommet fra de andre skure, var alle fremmede for Pierre og langt bedre klædt end ham. De betragtede ham og hans sko mistroisk, som en fremmed. Ikke langt fra ham gik en tyk major med et gustent, opsvulmet, vredt ansigt, iført en kasansk slobrok bundet med et håndklæde, og som tydeligvis nød sine medfangers respekt. Han holdt den ene hånd, hvori han klemte sin tobakspung, inden for slobrokkens bryst og holdt sin pibestilk fast med den anden. Pustende og hvæsende brummede majoren ad alle og enhver, fordi han mente, at han blev skubbet, og at alle havde travlt, selvom der ikke var noget at have travlt med, og at alle var forbavsede over noget, selvom der ikke var noget at forbavse sig over. En anden, en tynd lille officer, talte med alle og gættede på, hvor de nu blev ført hen, og hvor langt de ville nå den dag. En embedsmand i filtstøvler og kommissariatuniform løb frem og tilbage og betragtede Moskvas ruiner, mens han højlydt meddelte sine iagttagelser om, hvad der var brændt ned, og hvilken bydel de kunne se. En tredje officer, der efter sin accent at dømme var polak, skændtes med kommissariatsembedsmanden om, at han tog fejl af Moskvas forskellige kvarterer.

»Hvad skændes I om?« sagde majoren vredt. »Hvad forskel gør det, om det er Skt. Nikolaj eller Skt. Blasius? I kan se, det er brændt ned, og dermed basta.... Hvad skubber I for? Er vejen ikke bred nok?« sagde han til en mand bag ham, der slet ikke skubbede til ham.

»Åh, åh, åh! Hvad har de gjort?« hørte man fangerne sige fra alle sider, mens de stirrede på de forkullede ruiner. »Alt hinsides floden, og Zubova og i Kreml.... Se bare! Der er ikke halvdelen tilbage. Ja, det sagde jeg jo — hele kvarteret hinsides floden, og sådan er det.«
»Nå, I ved jo, det er brændt ned, så hvad nytter det at tale om det?« sagde majoren.
Da de passerede nær en kirke i Khamovniki — et af de få ubrændte kvarterer i Moskva — rykkede hele fangeskaren pludselig til side, og udbrud af rædsel og afsky hørtes.
»Åh, de skurke! Hvilke hedninger! Ja — død, død, det er han... Og smurt ind i noget!«

Pierre nærmede sig også kirken, hvor det syn var, der fremkaldte disse udbrud, og skimtede utydeligt noget, der lænede sig op ad kirkegårdens stakit. Ud fra kammeraternes ord — de kunne se bedre end ham — forstod han, at det var liget af en mand, stillet oprejst mod stakittet med ansigtet smurt ind i sod.

»Videre! For helvede... Videre! Tredive tusind djævle!...« begyndte eskortevagterne at bande, og de franske soldater drev med fornyet heftighed fangerne, der stirrede på den døde, bort med deres sabler.

english.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: The French evacuation began on the night between the sixth and seventh of October: kitchens and sheds were dismantled, carts loaded, and troops and baggage trains set off.

At seven in the morning, a French convoy in marching order—wearing shakos and carrying muskets, knapsacks, and enormous sacks—stood in front of the sheds. Animated French conversation mixed with curses sounded along the entire line.

In the shed, everyone was ready—dressed, belted, and wearing shoes—waiting only for the order to start. Only the sick soldier Sokolov, pale and thin with dark circles under his eyes, sat barefoot and undressed in his place. His eyes, prominent from the thinness of his face, gazed questioningly at his comrades, who paid no attention to him. He moaned regularly and quietly. It was clearly not so much his suffering that made him moan (he had dysentery) as his fear and grief at being left behind.
Pierre, with a rope tied around his waist and wearing shoes Karataev had made him from leather torn off a tea chest by a French soldier, went up to the sick man and crouched beside him.
'You know, Sokolov, they're not all leaving. There's a hospital here. You might actually be better off than the rest of us,' said Pierre.
'Oh Lord! Oh, it'll be the death of me! Oh Lord!' the man moaned louder.
'I'll go ask them again right now,' said Pierre, standing up and going to the shed door.

Just as Pierre reached the door, the corporal who had offered him a pipe the day before came up with two soldiers. The corporal and soldiers were in marching gear—knapsacks and shakos with metal chin straps—and these accessories made their familiar faces look completely different.
The corporal had come, on orders, to shut the door. The prisoners had to be counted before being let out.
'Corporal, what will they do with the sick man?...' Pierre began.

But even as he spoke, he began to doubt whether this was really the corporal he knew, or a stranger—so unlike himself did the man seem at that moment. Moreover, just as Pierre spoke, a sharp rattle of drums suddenly burst out from both sides. The corporal frowned at Pierre's words and, muttering some meaningless oaths, slammed the door shut. The shed went dark, and the sharp drum rattle drowned out the sick man's groans from both sides.

'There it is!... That force again!...' Pierre said to himself, and an involuntary shudder ran down his spine. In the corporal's transformed face, in the sound of his voice, in the stirring, deafening noise of the drums, Pierre recognized that mysterious, cold force that compelled people against their will to kill their fellow men—the force he had witnessed during the executions. To fear it, to try to escape it, to plead with or preach to those who served as its instruments was useless. Pierre understood this now. One could only wait and endure. He didn't go back to the sick man or turn to look at him, but stood frowning by the shed door.

When the door was opened and the prisoners, pressing against one another like a flock of sheep, squeezed through the exit, Pierre pushed forward and approached the very captain whom the corporal had assured him would do anything for him. The captain was also in marching gear, and on his cold face Pierre recognized that same force he had seen in the corporal's words and in the roll of the drums.
'Move along, move along!' the captain repeated, frowning sternly and scanning the prisoners streaming past him.
Pierre went up to him, though he knew the attempt would be useless.
'What is it?' the officer asked coldly, as if not recognizing Pierre.
Pierre told him about the sick man.
'He can walk, damn him!' said the captain. 'Move along, move along!' he continued without looking at Pierre.
'But he's dying,' Pierre began again.
'Would you be so good as to—' the captain shouted, his face darkening with anger.
'Drum-da-da-dum, dum-dum...' rattled the drums, and Pierre understood that this mysterious force had total control over these men and that there was no point saying anything more.
The officer prisoners were separated from the soldiers and told to march in front. There were about thirty officers, Pierre among them, and about three hundred soldiers.

The officers, who had come from other sheds, were all strangers to Pierre and much better dressed. They looked at him and his shoes with suspicion, as if he were an outsider. Not far from him walked a fat major with a sallow, bloated, angry face, wearing a Kazan dressing gown tied with a towel. He clearly commanded respect among his fellow prisoners. He kept one hand, clutching his tobacco pouch, inside the front of his dressing gown and held the stem of his pipe firmly with the other. Panting and puffing, the major grumbled at everyone, convinced he was being pushed and that they were all hurrying for no reason and amazed at nothing worth being amazed about. Another man, a thin little officer, talked to everyone, speculating about where they were being taken and how far they'd march that day. An official in felt boots and a commissariat uniform ran from side to side, pointing at the ruins of Moscow and loudly announcing what had burned and identifying different parts of the city. A third officer, a Pole by his accent, argued with the commissariat man about which neighborhood was which.

'What's the point of arguing?' said the major angrily. 'What does it matter if it's St. Nicholas or St. Blaise? It's burned down, and that's the end of it. What are you pushing for? Isn't the road wide enough?' he snapped at someone behind him who wasn't pushing at all.

'Oh, oh, oh! Look what they've done!' the prisoners murmured on all sides, gazing at the charred ruins. 'Everything beyond the river, and Zubovo, and the Kremlin... Just look! Not half of it left. Yes, I told you—the whole district beyond the river. That's how it is.'
'Well, you can see it's burned. What's the use of talking about it?' said the major.
As they passed a church in the Khamovniki district—one of the few unburned parts of Moscow—the whole crowd of prisoners suddenly recoiled, and exclamations of horror and disgust were heard.
'Oh, the monsters! What heathens! Yes—dead, dead he is... And his face is smeared with something!'

Pierre pushed forward toward the church where this sight was causing such outrage, and dimly made out something propped against the fence around the churchyard. From his companions who could see better, he learned it was a dead body, set upright against the railings with its face smeared with soot.
'Move on! What the devil... Move on! Thirty thousand devils!...' the guards cursed, and the French soldiers drove the crowd of staring prisoners away with fresh viciousness, swords in hand.
